chapter_title: Android Project Structure and Basic UI Components
chapter_summary:
Now that your Android development environment is set up, let's dive into the anatomy of an Android project. Understanding the project structure is crucial for navigating your codebase and knowing where to place different types of files. When you create a new project in Android Studio, it generates a hierarchical structure that, at first glance, might seem complex. However, we can break it down into key areas. The `app` module is where most of your application code and resources reside. Inside `app/src/main`, you'll find `java` (or `kotlin`) for your source code, and `res` for your application resources.

The `java` (or `kotlin`) directory contains your `.kt` or `.java` files, organized by package name. This is where your `Activity` classes, `Fragment` classes, and other logic-related code live. An **Activity** is a single, focused thing that the user can do. It typically represents a single screen in your application, providing a window in which to place your UI. For example, a login screen, a settings screen, or a photo gallery screen would each typically be implemented as an `Activity`. Every app has at least one `Activity`, usually the main entry point.

The `res` directory is a treasure trove of your application's non-code resources. It's further subdivided into directories like `drawable` (for images and XML drawables), `layout` (for XML files defining your UI layouts), `mipmap` (for launcher icons), `values` (for strings, colors, dimensions, and styles), and `font` (for custom fonts). Separating resources from code is a core principle of Android development, promoting maintainability and localization. For instance, putting all user-facing text in `res/values/strings.xml` allows you to easily translate your app into multiple languages without touching your code.

Two critical configuration files you'll encounter are `AndroidManifest.xml` and `build.gradle`. The **`AndroidManifest.xml`** file is the manifest of your application. It describes the fundamental characteristics of your app and defines each of its components (activities, services, broadcast receivers, content providers). It declares permissions the app needs (e.g., internet access, camera), hardware and software features it requires, and specifies the entry point of your app. Without a properly configured `AndroidManifest.xml`, your app cannot run. For example, if your app needs to access the internet, you must declare `<uses-permission android:name="android.permission.INTERNET"/>` within this file. Forgetting to declare necessary permissions is a common mistake that leads to runtime errors or features simply not working.

The **`build.gradle`** files (there's one for the project and one for the app module) are configuration files for the Gradle build system. They specify dependencies (external libraries your app uses), the Android SDK versions to compile against, and various build settings. For instance, to include a library like `androidx.constraintlayout:constraintlayout`, you'd add `implementation 'androidx.constraintlayout:constraintlayout:2.1.4'` to your app's `build.gradle` file under the `dependencies` block. Understanding these files is key to managing your project's external libraries and build process.

Now, let's talk about building user interfaces. Android's UI is constructed using a hierarchy of **`View`** and **`ViewGroup`** objects. A `View` is the basic building block for user interface components, like a button or a text field. A `ViewGroup` is a special type of `View` that can contain other `View`s and `ViewGroup`s, acting as a container or layout manager.

Some fundamental `View` components include:
*   **`TextView`**: Displays static text. You can set its text, color, size, and other properties.
*   **`Button`**: A clickable element that performs an action when tapped.
*   **`EditText`**: An editable text field where users can input data.

To arrange these `View`s on a screen, we use `ViewGroup`s, commonly referred to as **layouts**.
*   **`LinearLayout`**: Arranges its children in a single row or column. You specify the `android:orientation` attribute as either `horizontal` or `vertical`. This is excellent for simple, linear arrangements.
*   **`RelativeLayout`**: Positions its children relative to each other or to the parent layout. For example, you can center a `Button` or place a `TextView` below another `TextView`. While powerful, it can become complex for intricate UIs.

Here's a simple XML example for a `LinearLayout` with a `TextView` and a `Button`:

```xml
<!-- res/layout/activity_main.xml -->
<LinearLayout
    xmlns:android="http://schemas.android.com/apk/res/android"
    xmlns:tools="http://schemas.android.com/tools"
    android:layout_width="match_parent"
    android:layout_height="match_parent"
    android:orientation="vertical"
    android:gravity="center"
    tools:context=".MainActivity">

    <TextView
        android:id="@+id/welcomeTextView"
        android:layout_width="wrap_content"
        android:layout_height="wrap_content"
        android:text="Welcome to My App!"
        android:textSize="24sp"
        android:padding="16dp" />

    <Button
        android:id="@+id/actionButton"
        android:layout_width="wrap_content"
        android:layout_height="wrap_content"
        android:text="Click Me"
        android:layout_marginTop="24dp" />

</LinearLayout>
```

In this example, `android:layout_width` and `android:layout_height` are crucial attributes, typically set to `match_parent` (to fill the parent) or `wrap_content` (to size itself to its content). `android:id` provides a unique identifier for the view, allowing you to reference it in your Kotlin/Java code. `android:gravity="center"` on the `LinearLayout` centers its children.

Understanding the difference between `match_parent` and `wrap_content` is a common point of confusion for beginners. `match_parent` (or `fill_parent` in older APIs) makes the view as big as its parent, while `wrap_content` makes the view just big enough to contain its content. Misusing these can lead to unexpected UI layouts. Always preview your layouts in Android Studio's Design editor to catch issues early.

screens.title: Android Project Structure & Basic UI Components
screens.subtitle: Where files live, what an Activity is, and how simple Views and layouts assemble a screen

narration.text: Welcome. In this lesson you will learn the anatomy of a standard Android project and the basic UI building blocks you will use every day. We’ll map the folders and files Android Studio creates, explain the roles of AndroidManifest. xml and build. gradle, and describe how Activities, Views, and ViewGroups combine to form a usable screen. You will also see a concrete example: a simple login layout built with a LinearLayout, two EditText fields, and a Button. Understanding where code belongs matters because it helps you locate resources, configure permissions, and manage dependencies without guesswork. A common early mistake is editing resources as if they were code: remember that strings and colors belong in res/values so you can localize and theme your app. By the end of this board you’ll be able to identify the app/src/main tree, explain what goes in res, spot the manifest and Gradle files, and construct a simple form layout. Think about one screen in an app you use daily — you’ll soon know which files to open to change that screen.

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: Project structure separates code, resources, and configuration so you can edit UI, logic, and build settings independently.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: Skills you will master in this chapter

narration.text: In this chapter you will develop four concrete skills that let you navigate an Android project and design simple screens. First, you will learn to find and interpret the essential directories and files inside a typical project so you know where code and assets belong. That helps you make targeted edits without breaking the build. Second, you will learn to differentiate the roles of AndroidManifest. xml and build. gradle files, and why declaring components, permissions, and dependencies in the right file matters for runtime behavior. Third, you will learn what an Activity is and how it represents a single focused screen; you will practice identifying which Activity should host a given UI. Fourth, you will design simple user interfaces using core Views and layouts, learning to use TextView, Button, EditText and basic containers like LinearLayout and RelativeLayout. Each objective includes a small mnemonic to help you remember where to look and a verified competency milestone so you know when you are ready to move on.

screens.title: Project root and the app module
screens.subtitle: Where your application code and resources live

narration.text: Let’s walk through the app module — the heart of most Android projects. When you create a project in Android Studio you will see a top-level project folder and an app module folder beneath it. The app module contains app/src/main which splits into two important areas: the source folder (java or kotlin) and the res folder for resources. The source folder is organized by package name and contains Activities, Fragments, and other classes. The res folder contains non-code assets such as layouts, drawables, mipmap icons, and values like strings and colors. This separation is intentional: source code compiles into classes, while resources are packaged and referenced by identifiers. A concrete example: if you need to change a button label for translation, you edit res/values/strings. xml, not the Kotlin file. A common misconception is that image assets should live alongside source files; instead, put images in res/drawable and launcher icons in res/mipmap. Finally, being able to identify app/src/main quickly prevents you from editing files in the wrong module when a project contains multiple modules. Consider the difference between code changes and resource changes as different maintenance lanes — knowing the lanes saves time and prevents build errors.

keyIdea.title: Where to work
keyIdea.text: app/src/main holds your code (java/kotlin) and resources (res); edit strings in values and code in source folders.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Project Anatomy
app/src/main
This module tree is the standard workspace for your app logic and assets. Inside you will always find the source folder and res folder.
Source (java / kotlin)
Contains Activities, Fragments, and other classes organized by package name.
res (resources)
Layouts, drawables, mipmap, values, and fonts — used by the UI and packaged with the app.
Key Takeaway

Edit UI text in values/strings, change layout structure in res/layout, and write behavior in java or kotlin files.

Visual file map
res/layout
XML layout files that define how screens are structured.
res/drawable
Images and XML drawables used by the UI.
res/values
Strings, colors, dimensions, and styles for consistent design and localization.
res/mipmap
Launcher icons for different screen densities.
Common mistake
Placing translatable text directly in layout XML instead of using res/values/strings.xml makes localization harder and is a frequent beginner error.

screens.title: AndroidManifest.xml — the app manifest
screens.subtitle: What it declares and why it must be correct

narration.text: The AndroidManifest. xml is the application manifest — a required XML file that declares the app’s components, permissions, and essential features. It lists each Activity, Service, BroadcastReceiver, and ContentProvider so the system knows what exists inside your app. It also declares permissions such as internet access, camera, or location, which are gatekeepers that the OS enforces at install time or runtime. For example, if your app needs to access the internet but you forget to add the internet permission to the manifest, network requests can fail or cause runtime errors. A common beginner misconception is that permissions declared in code are sufficient; they must also be declared in the manifest. The manifest also specifies the app’s entry point with an intent-filter on the main Activity. Practically, when you add a new Activity class, remember to register it in the manifest or the app may not navigate correctly. If your app targets newer APIs, some permissions require runtime requests, but declaration in the manifest remains the first and necessary step. The manifest is therefore both a registry and a contract between your app and the platform.

keyIdea.title: Manifest role
keyIdea.text: AndroidManifest.xml registers components and permissions; missing declarations often cause runtime failures.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › AndroidManifest.xml
What the manifest describes
  • App components: activities, services, broadcast receivers, and providers.
  • Permissions required by the app, declared with <uses-permission> tags.
  • Hardware and software features your app expects, helping the Play Store filter installs.
  • Entry point: the Activity with the MAIN action and LAUNCHER category.
Common mistake

Forgetting to declare a required permission in the manifest causes security exceptions or silent feature failures at runtime.

Example
To request internet access you must add this line inside the manifest root:
<uses-permission android:name="android.permission.INTERNET"/>
Why it matters
The manifest is checked before your app runs and is part of what the platform uses to grant access and list app capabilities to the system.

narration.text: Gradle build files control how your Android project compiles and which external libraries are included. There is usually a project-level build. gradle that holds global build settings and repositories, and a module-level build. gradle inside the app module that lists dependencies, compile SDK versions, and module-specific build options. For example, to include the ConstraintLayout library you add an implementation line to the module build. gradle dependencies block. A practical outcome is that adding or updating a dependency here changes what classes are available to your application code. A common beginner error is to place dependency lines in the project build. gradle instead of the module build. gradle; the module-level file is where implementation and api dependencies belong for compilation. Build settings like minSdkVersion and targetSdkVersion also live in the module configuration; changing them affects device compatibility and available APIs. When you change Gradle files, Android Studio may sync the project, fetch libraries, and recompile — so treat Gradle edits as build-time actions. Understanding which file controls which scope helps you manage dependencies and avoid build failures. build.gradle files means use project-level build.gradle for global settings; use module-level build.gradle to declare dependencies and sdk versions.. In practical terms, project-level and module-level build configuration. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Gradle purpose
keyIdea.text: Use project-level build.gradle for global settings; use module-level build.gradle to declare dependencies and SDK versions.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › build.gradle
What goes where
  • Project-level build.gradle: repositories and classpath plugins used across modules.
  • Module-level build.gradle: dependencies, compileSdkVersion, minSdkVersion, and build types.
  • Add libraries to dependencies with implementation lines so classes become available at compile time.
Pro tip

When adding a library, sync Gradle and watch the build output for resolution errors — they often indicate version conflicts or missing repositories.

Example dependency
implementation 'androidx.constraintlayout:constraintlayout:2.1.4'
Why it matters
Dependencies declared in the module build.gradle determine which libraries are bundled and compiled into your app. Put them in the right file to avoid build problems.

screens.title: Activity — a focused screen
screens.subtitle: What an Activity represents and how to choose one

narration.text: An Activity is the fundamental unit that represents a single, focused thing the user can do — usually a screen. Think of an Activity as the container that hosts Views and ViewGroups and coordinates user interaction. For instance, a login screen, a photo gallery screen, and a settings screen are typically each an Activity. An important practical note is that every app must declare at least one Activity, often the main entry point. When designing your app, decide whether a UI belongs to an Activity or should be a reusable Fragment or component; the chapter focuses on Activities as screens. A common misconception is to treat Activities as lightweight view holders; in fact they often manage navigation, lifecycle-aware components, and interactions between UI and business logic. In practice, when you create a new screen, add an Activity class in the source folder and register it in AndroidManifest. xml. A concrete example is creating a LoginActivity that inflates activity_main. xml and handles text input and the login button tap. As you build more screens, keeping a clear mapping between Activity classes and screens makes debugging and navigation predictable.

keyIdea.title: Activity definition
keyIdea.text: An Activity represents a single screen and hosts the UI; register it in the manifest and implement UI interactions in its class.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Activity
Activity as a screen
An Activity provides a window for UI and handles user interaction for a single focused task. It typically inflates a layout resource and responds to UI events.
Example
LoginActivity inflates activity_main.xml, reads the username and password fields, and handles the login button tap.
Common misconception
Do not confuse an Activity with a single view. Activities host many views and coordinate logic beyond layout.
Checklist
  • Create an Activity class in the source package.
  • Inflate the layout resource with setContentView in onCreate.
  • Register the Activity in AndroidManifest.xml.
Scenario
You need a screen for user profile editing. Create a ProfileActivity, design res/layout/activity_profile.xml, and register ProfileActivity in the manifest so the system can start it.
Key Takeaway

Map screens to Activity classes and register them to make the app navigable and maintainable.

narration.text: Android UI is constructed from two fundamental concepts: Views and ViewGroups. A View is a single UI element, such as a TextView, Button, or EditText. It is responsible for drawing itself and handling simple user interaction such as taps or text entry. A ViewGroup is a special View that can contain other Views and ViewGroups; it acts as a container and controls how its children are arranged. For example, LinearLayout arranges children in a single row or column, while RelativeLayout positions children relative to one another or to the parent. The distinction matters because layout and arrangement logic belongs in ViewGroups; individual Views should focus on rendering and input. A common beginner error is to use many nested ViewGroups for spacing rather than using correct layout attributes — this can impact performance. A practical example: to make a login form you use EditText Views for username and password and a Button View for submission, all placed inside a LinearLayout ViewGroup with vertical orientation. Remember: Views are content, ViewGroups are the layout managers that position that content. When designing, favor simple layouts that communicate structure clearly and avoid unnecessary nesting.

keyIdea.title: UI building blocks
keyIdea.text: Views render content and handle input; ViewGroups arrange children and manage layout behavior.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › View & ViewGroup
Core distinction
Views are individual UI controls. ViewGroups are containers that arrange those controls. Use ViewGroups to control layout and Views for content and interaction.
Views
TextView, Button, EditText — display or receive input.
ViewGroups
LinearLayout, RelativeLayout — arrange children with rules and attributes.
Performance note
Minimize unnecessary nesting of ViewGroups to keep layouts performant and easier to maintain.
Concrete example
A login form: two EditText views to capture username and password and a Button to submit, arranged by a LinearLayout that stacks them vertically.
Key Takeaway

Separate layout concerns (ViewGroups) from content (Views) and avoid deep nesting for clarity and performance.

screens.title: Simple LinearLayout example
screens.subtitle: XML that builds a centered login UI

narration.text: We’ll walk through a concrete XML layout example that builds a simple, centered login screen using LinearLayout. The layout uses match_parent for the root dimensions so it fills the available window and sets android:orientation to vertical. Inside we place a TextView for the title, then a Button. Attributes like android:layout_width and android:layout_height control sizing, and android:gravity centers content. Notice the use of android:id to reference views from code and android:hint on EditText to provide placeholder text for users. A common confusion is when to use match_parent versus wrap_content: match_parent makes a view as large as the parent, while wrap_content sizes a view to its content. In login forms you often use match_parent on input fields so they span available width and wrap_content for the text label. Now inspect the XML snippet shown — it is the minimal structure you will copy into res/layout/activity_main. xml during the hands-on activity. After saving, preview in Android Studio to see immediate visual feedback. If the TextView or Button does not appear centered, check gravity attributes and ensure the root LinearLayout uses android:gravity="center". Try changing textSize in the title to observe how the design shifts — this is a useful interactive experiment in Android Studio.

keyIdea.title: XML example
keyIdea.text: A LinearLayout with vertical orientation centers a title, inputs, and a button to form a simple login screen. Use ids and hints for code and UX.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Login Layout XML
XML snippet (place in res/layout/activity_main.xml)
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="utf-8"?>
<LinearLayout
    xmlns:android="http://schemas.android.com/apk/res/android"
    xmlns:tools="http://schemas.android.com/tools"
    android:layout_width="match_parent"
    android:layout_height="match_parent"
    android:orientation="vertical"
    android:gravity="center"
    android:padding="16dp"
    tools:context=".MainActivity">

    <TextView
        android:id="@+id/welcomeTextView"
        android:layout_width="wrap_content"
        android:layout_height="wrap_content"
        android:text="Welcome to My App!"
        android:textSize="24sp"
        android:padding="16dp" />

    <Button
        android:id="@+id/actionButton"
        android:layout_width="wrap_content"
        android:layout_height="wrap_content"
        android:text="Click Me"
        android:layout_marginTop="24dp" />

</LinearLayout>
Explanation
  • Root LinearLayout fills the screen and centers its children with android:gravity="center".
  • TextView uses wrap_content so it sizes to the text; Button also wraps by default.
  • IDs allow the Activity to find views and wire logic in code.
Try this

Change textSize in the TextView and preview the layout to observe live updates in Android Studio.

screens.title: LinearLayout vs RelativeLayout
screens.subtitle: When to use each layout type

narration.text: Two common layout containers you will use are LinearLayout and RelativeLayout. LinearLayout arranges children sequentially in a single row or column. It is straightforward and ideal for simple stacked forms, like a vertical login screen. You set android:orientation to horizontal or vertical and then control spacing with layout margins and gravity. RelativeLayout, on the other hand, positions children relative to each other or the parent. It is more flexible when you want to place a View below, to the right of, or centered relative to another view without strict nesting. A practical example: for a list of preferences a vertical LinearLayout is the simplest solution. For a toolbar where a title must be centered and buttons must align left and right, RelativeLayout helps avoid extra nesting. A common misconception is that RelativeLayout is always better because it is more powerful; in reality it can become complex and harder to maintain. Choose LinearLayout for simple, linear arrangements and RelativeLayout when relative positioning simplifies the structure or reduces nesting. Start simple, then refactor to RelativeLayout if alignment needs force it. LinearLayout vs RelativeLayout means use linearlayout for simple vertical or horizontal stacks; use relativelayout for positioning views relative to each other or the parent.. In practical terms, when to use each layout type. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Layout choice
keyIdea.text: Use LinearLayout for simple vertical or horizontal stacks; use RelativeLayout for positioning views relative to each other or the parent.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Layout Comparison
LinearLayout
Arranges children in a row or column. Use android:orientation to control direction and android:gravity for alignment. Best for simple, ordered layouts like forms.
Pros: Simple, predictable, easy to read.
Cons: Can require nesting for complex arrangements.
RelativeLayout
Positions children relative to one another or the parent. Useful when you need overlap or specific alignment without deep nesting.
Pros: Flexible positioning, can reduce nesting.
Cons: Can become hard to maintain if rules become complex.
Scenario guidance
If you need a straight list of items, use LinearLayout. If you must position elements relative to each other — for example, anchor one view below another and align another to the parent edge — RelativeLayout may simplify the layout. Always preview and refactor to maintain readability.

narration.text: Three Views you will use constantly are TextView, Button, and EditText. TextView displays static or styled text and supports attributes such as textSize, textColor, and padding. Button is a clickable control that triggers actions; visually it resembles a TextView but with click handling and typical styling. EditText is an editable view where users enter text; it supports inputType to restrict input to email, password, number, and other formats, and android:hint to show placeholder text. A concrete example is a login form where two EditText fields collect username and password and a Button triggers authentication. Important attributes include android:id to reference the view programmatically and android:layout_width and android:layout_height to control sizing. Beginners sometimes forget to set inputType on password fields, resulting in visible text; use inputType="textPassword" to obscure the input. Also use android:hint for improved usability rather than pre-filling text. Finally, remember to reference strings in res/values/strings. xml to make translation straightforward. These small attribute choices noticeably improve UX and maintainability. Common Views: TextView, Button, EditText means textview shows text, button handles taps, edittext accepts input — use ids, inputtype, and hints to make controls usable and localizable.. In practical terms, purpose and typical attributes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: View attributes
keyIdea.text: TextView shows text, Button handles taps, EditText accepts input — use ids, inputType, and hints to make controls usable and localizable.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Common Views
TextView
Displays text. Use textSize, textColor, and padding. Prefer strings.xml for text content to support localization.
EditText
Editable text input. Use android:hint for placeholder and android:inputType to control keyboard and masking for passwords.
Button
Clickable control that performs an action. Style with padding and margin and wire click behavior from your Activity code.
Example attributes
  • android:id="@+id/editTextUsername" — unique identifier for code references.
  • android:layout_width="match_parent" — often used for input fields to span available width.
  • android:inputType="textPassword" — obscures input for passwords.
Common mistake
Leaving user-facing text in layout XML instead of strings.xml reduces the ability to localize the app. Use resource strings for labels and placeholders.

screens.title: Hands-on: Build the Simple Login UI
screens.subtitle: Step-by-step instructions to create and preview the layout

narration.text: This hands-on process walks through creating a basic login UI using LinearLayout. Step one: open activity_main. xml in app/src/main/res/layout. Replace the root layout with a LinearLayout set to vertical orientation and center gravity. Step two: add a TextView for the title, two EditText views for username and password, and a Button for login. Set android:id on each view so the Activity can reference them and use android:hint to guide the user. narration.text: Understanding android:layout_width and android:layout_height is essential to predictable layouts. match_parent makes a view as large as its parent; wrap_content sizes the view just large enough for its content. Use match_parent for input fields that should span the full width of the available area, and wrap_content for labels and buttons that should size to their text. Another required attribute is android:id which gives a unique identifier to a view so code can reference it via findViewById or view binding. For example, when you need to read the username text from an EditText you reference its id in your Activity code. A common beginner error is mixing up match_parent and wrap_content, which can lead to views unintentionally filling the screen or collapsing. Always preview after changing layout attributes. Also prefer resource references for padding, strings, and colors to promote reuse and consistency. The practical habit is: set sensible default sizing, use ids for code interaction, and centralize UI text in strings. xml for easier translation and maintenance. content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Sizing & IDs
Sizing attributes
match_parent expands to fill the parent; wrap_content sizes to the content. Use match_parent on inputs to give consistent alignment and wrap_content for labels and icon buttons.
android:id
Assign a unique id so your Activity code can find the view for reading input or wiring click handlers.
Concrete example
<EditText
    android:id="@+id/editTextUsername"
    android:layout_width="match_parent"
    android:layout_height="wrap_content"
    android:hint="Username" />

<Button
    android:id="@+id/buttonLogin"
    android:layout_width="wrap_content"
    android:layout_height="wrap_content"
    android:text="Login" />
Misconception check
Do not assume ids are optional — without ids you cannot reference views from code. And don’t overuse match_parent where wrap_content is appropriate, as it may break your intended layout.

First, the app module under app/src/main separates source code from resources — java or kotlin files live alongside a res directory that holds layouts, drawables, and values. Third, build. gradle files control build configuration and dependencies; module-level Gradle is where you add implementation dependencies and specify SDK versions. narration.text: Three quick reminders as you practice. First, separate resources from code: use res for layouts and values so strings and assets are easy to change and translate. Second, always declare necessary permissions in AndroidManifest. xml before relying on platform features to prevent runtime security exceptions. Third, prefer simple layouts: start with LinearLayout for stacked content and only use RelativeLayout when relative positioning simplifies the structure. These rules will keep your projects organized, reduce errors, and make UIs easier to maintain as you add screens and features.
